subject: stainedGlassPeacock
pitch:
Category: Animal.
Subject: peacock with fanned tail.
Style: stained glass with lead came.
reasoning:
I'm planning a module for a stained-glass peacock with a fanned tail, using lead-came style with Worley-cell jewel-toned panels separated by dark lines, aiming for roughly 600-800 well-crafted lines since this needs to be correct in one pass.

Now I'm sketching the physical proportions: body around 1m long with the head reaching ~1.0m height, legs ~0.4m, and a tail fan spanning roughly 1.5-2m wide and 1.2m tall, centered behind the hips and fanning upward in a vertical plane. I'm working out the angular span of the fan so its lowest tips stay near ground level given the chosen radius and center height, aiming for something like a -100° to 100° spread from vertical.

For the rig, I'm planning a hierarchy starting at the hips joint, branching into spine, neck, head, and jaw chains, plus leg chains with toe digits, and separate wing chains that stay modestly spread outward and back from the body rather than tucked. For the tail train, I'm treating it as a ring of feather groups arranged radially around a frame at the tail base oriented forward, so angle zero points upward and the feathers radiate outward to form the fan shape.

I'm giving the fan a wide angular range (roughly -100° to 100°) with a slight positive tilt so the whole display curves concavely toward the viewer, like a real peacock train. Each ring item will have feathers swept outward from its point with varying lengths, since real peacock trains layer longer eye-tipped feathers with shorter ones beneath.

I'll build three concentric rows: outer (~26 feathers, length 1.05), middle (~22, length 0.78, slightly forward), and inner (~18, length 0.52). Each feather gets a thin gold/bronze rachis, a stained-glass-painted leaf-shaped vane, and a glowing eyespot card at the tip rendered as layered almond rings (bronze/gold, green, teal, deep blue) with dark lead lines, boosted glow strength since it's meant to look backlit, and double-sided for visibility from any angle.

For placement, I'm positioning each eye card using a frame near the feather tip, with the card growing outward along the shaft and its face oriented along the flow direction so it reads correctly when viewed from downstream.

Thinking through vanes now: 66 feathers means 132 parts if I split shaft and vane separately, but painted vanes can't glow, so I'm considering drawing the whole feather — shaft, barbs, and eye — as one double-sided glowing card texture instead, like a stained-glass panel with sparse barbs near the base.

With 26 feathers spread across 200° at radius 1.0, the gap between tips is tighter than card width, causing overlap and z-fighting near the tips. Rather than relying on the ring generator, I'll compute each feather's position manually and stagger their depth to avoid flickering.

I decide to use `item.moved(point)` so each feather keeps its original bone and orientation while shifting its base point by an alternating parity offset along the depth axis, since switching to raw frames from tuples would lose the bone reference needed for proper tail rigging.

For richness I'm considering adding a small cabochon jewel sphere at each outer feather's eye, budgeting roughly 26 outer shaft+cabochon pairs, 22 mid shafts, and 18 inner shafts (~100 parts total), plus a lead-came style arc frame connecting feathers at each radius for structure.

Those arcs would cross over the cards and not follow joint rotation unless rigged to the hip bone, so I'll scale back and just add one short rigid arc near the base (r=0.18) to form a semicircular "rose" of covert feathers under the tail base.

For the body I'm planning the peacock's color scheme: iridescent royal blue stained-glass cells on the neck and breast, bronze-green scales on the back, barred cream/black wing coverts with rufous primaries, a wiry crested head with blue-tipped pom-poms, white eye stripes, grey-brown beak and legs.

Writing stained-glass paint function...

For texel density, I'm estimating body surface area around 2 m² and working out that a 2048px paint sheet gives crisp lead lines for the ~4mm cell size with lead width.

I also want highlight streaks inside each pane using noise-based mottling, plus ripple effects for the cathedral glass look. I'm deciding against modeling actual lead came ridges as 3D geometry since that's too complex — instead I'll paint lead lines and add extra 3D outlines only on key edges like the wing, beak, and crest, then start laying out concrete body coordinates with the bird facing +Z and hips as the root joint.

Now I'm sketching out proportions: the body ovoid runs from rump to breast with the neck curving up to a small head, then I'm pushing toward a stylized chunkier look with a bigger head and slender S-curved neck, and working out leg placement with hips tucked into the body and a long tarsus leading down to the feet.

For the legs, I'm planning a three-segment chain (femur, tibiotarsus, tarsometatarsus) with the knee bending forward and the ankle bending back to get natural bird-leg posture, then adding toes as simple joint chains branching from the ankle tip, with three forward and one back toe sized to the foot radius.

Now I'm shifting to the spine chain, mapping points from the hips up through the lower and upper back toward the chest to define that joint path.

Continuing upward, I'm building the neck chain from the chest with a smooth curve of three joints leading to the head and jaw joints at the top, parented appropriately. Then I'm addressing the tail: adding a "tailBase" joint at the rump, parented to the hips, angled backward and upward, marking its role as "tail" for the rig.

For the body loft itself, I'm planning the path of stations from the rump through the hips to the chest, deciding which joints should own which segments of the mesh -- since tailBase has no child joint, I need to be careful about how its projection works, so I'm leaning toward a simpler bone list of just hips and spine for the main loft.

Deciding the hips joint owns the rump since it projects before the spine chain starts. For the neck, I'll sweep it as its own smooth chain starting inside the chest and tapering from a thicker base to a narrower point near the head, with the head itself as a sphere. Now I'm working out the loft stations with full width and height values.

I'm designing a stained-glass style paint function that assigns color per cell based on region position and normal, with blue for breast, bronze-green for back, dark for belly. For the wings, I'm planning folded chains with shoulder and elbow joints positioned slightly drooping for a display pose.

Rather than fully folded against the body, I'm considering spreading the wings outward and back, with joints from shoulder to tip angling wider and lower, so they sit in front of the fanned tail without clashing with it visually.

Actually, peacocks naturally droop their wings open during display, revealing rufous primaries - so I'll use that as the rest pose, naming the wing bone chain shoulder/elbow/wrist/tip with a "wing" role. For the surface, I'm planning a covert membrane barred cream and black between the wing bones and a trailing edge, with rufous primary feathers extruded as blades fanning backward from the wrist and darker secondaries closer in.

I'm setting feather y-direction along the wing span, keeping the blade outline symmetric about its axis, and letting membrane and tube elements inherit bending from the chain's span joints by default unless a bone is explicitly specified. I'm also placing the head joint relative to the body region.

Now I'm defining the skull sphere with a royal-blue glass finish and smaller surface cells, then layering decals for the facial pattern -- white crescents above and below the eye to mimic a peacock's bare facial skin -- plus a detailed eye decal with iris, gold ring, and highlight, while pushing eye placement slightly toward the front for better visibility despite the real bird's side-set eyes.

Working out the beak geometry now, shaping the upper and lower mandibles as flattened cones attached to the head and jaw joints, figuring out how local scale and axis orientation interact when the part aims forward.

For the crest, I'm thinking through how to represent the peacock's fan of feathers rising from the crown, and whether it spreads front-to-back or side-to-side like a real crest.

For the crest tips I'll use small glowing pale-blue teardrop shapes rendered as cross cards so they read from every angle. For the body I'm planning cobalt blue glass cells on the neck and breast, bronze-green scale-like texture on the back, and a barred palette for the wing coverts.

For the legs I'm using grey-brown horn material with lead-grey scute detailing and basic toe shapes, with feathered dark grey-brown capsules for the thighs. For the tail fan base I'm building a layered structure of short eye-feathers around the "rose" center, using four layers with decreasing lengths and feather counts to build up the dense inner coverts.

Writing feather placement logic...

I'm working out the fan's tilt geometry, wanting it to lean back slightly and cup forward like a real peacock's tail, then positioning the fan's center relative to the tailBase joint.

Checking the fan radius and height against the rump: the top reaches about 1.87m which is close enough to a real bird's proportions. I'm verifying the forward-tilted feather tips don't collide with the body, since the rump sits around z=-0.32 and the tips swing forward to roughly z=-0.08, with side tips extending well past the wing width.

Comparing wing tip position against fan clearance, there's a near-clash of about 4cm, so I'm reducing the fan tilt and repositioning the wing joints—shoulder, elbow, wrist, and tip—to droop more forward and down, keeping the primaries clear of the fan.

That feather base sits fine inside the rump tip. For the feather card itself, I'm designing each one with a shaft running down the center, sparse glassy barbs growing denser near the top, and an eye pattern built from nested almond and ring shapes—bronze, green, gold, teal—with a kidney-shaped blue heart outlined in dark lead strokes sized to stay crisp at the final raster resolution.

I'm keeping it simple by using one eye texture for most feathers, with sword-shaped tailless feathers reserved for the outermost lower pair on each side, and sizing each card at roughly a 0.3 width-to-length ratio to match the drawing's proportions.

Checking the math though, a full 1.15m card at that ratio makes the eye way too wide relative to real feather eyes, and with 27 feathers spread over 200° the spacing gets too tight to avoid heavy overlap. So instead I'll shrink the card to width 0.2 and length 0.62, placing it near the tip of the shaft so it only covers the eye portion, letting the shaft itself represent the rest of the feather's length with barbs fading out below the card.

I'm alternating z-offsets slightly between neighboring feathers to prevent z-fighting flicker, orienting each card so its base sits at the shaft root and its eye faces outward, and scaling the card size by L for the lower feather layers. For the shaft itself I'm drawing a tapered spike along the feather's outward axis in a dark lead-came color to represent the metal structure.

Now I'm settling on a slightly lighter grey-brown tone for the lead came to add some shading contrast, and placing small flat-blue cabochon jewel spheres at each eye center on the outer and middle layers, positioning them using the item's local coordinate frame so they sit just forward of the card surface along its tilt direction.

I'll set sink to 0 for precision, so the eye center lands near the root plus roughly 77.5% of the card length along the outward facing direction, with a small forward offset that I can mostly ignore. The card's frame stands along that outward axis, with its face oriented by the flow direction pointing toward the front.

For lighting, the facing axis doubles as the normal, so top feathers catch more light while lower ones sit darker, though the glow strength overrides this anyway since it's set to full brightness. The glass body paints can't glow on their own, so I'm leaning toward saturated, vivid colors to keep that stained-glass luminosity feel.

Now I'm working out the ring rig function's parameters, where angles are measured counter-clockwise around the line's axis starting from world-up, running symmetrically between -100 and 100 degrees.

For joint naming I'm using sequential labels like "trainA1", "trainA2" to keep them unique across rings. For the toes, I'm setting up individual digit joints parented to the foot, aimed at each toe tip, then sweeping small capsule tubes between foot and toe positions sized to just touch the floor.

For the leg itself, I'm sweeping a capsule chain through hip, knee, ankle, and foot, with the thigh portion hidden inside the body feathers and a darker "trouser" capsule covering the upper leg down past the knee, before computing the actual limb root position for IK.

Toe tip aims along the foot's downward tangent with toes parented to footL, and I'm adding small spurs on the back of the tarsus for detail. I'm painting the tarsus scutes with stained-glass-style lead lines for consistency, then sizing the head sphere using local scale factors to set width and length proportions.

Now I'm designing the face: placing eye decals on the skull surface, then building an SVG facial pattern with crescent stripes above and below the eye, a dark glossy iris with a gold ring and lead outlines, mirrored appropriately for each side of the head.

I'm sketching the beak as a simple cone with a lower jaw and tiny nostril, using a horn-grey color, then planning the crest as a ring of spikes rotated around a sideways axis spanning roughly a 90-degree arc, aiming for about 11 shafts to approximate a peacock's crest.

Writing crest geometry...

For the body, I'm thinking through the neck-to-breast transition with a seamless paint, adding glass gloss, and shaping the back feathers as scale-like panels to mimic the bronze-green peacock pattern. I'm also considering an eye-jewel sphere and a boss medallion where the fan feathers converge at the tail base, mostly hidden from front view but visible from behind.

Now I'm working out the brown spike feathers behind the fan, explicitly assigning them to the tailBase bone since sweep options support that, then moving on to mirror the wing feather construction for both sides using a parametric point function.

For the wings I'm setting up each side's joint chain—shoulder, elbow, wrist, wingTip—parented to the spine joint, then sweeping the arm bones with a covert-feather colored tube. Now I'm defining the membrane surface between the leading-edge chain and a trailing set of points positioned behind and below it.

Defining feather extrusion geometry...

I'll offset each blade slightly along its normal to avoid z-fighting, then move to covert paint: barred cream and dark brown-black panes to mimic a peacock's barred coverts, avoiding colors that would merge with the lead lines. Now I'm writing a glass helper function that generates paint regions based on cell position, seed, and lead width.

Writing glass shader logic...

Mapping out the rest of the body regions — bronze-green for the back, dark tones for the belly — with noisy boundaries so the color transitions don't look like straight lines, and using smaller cell sizes for the neck and head versus the body.

Legs get a muted horn palette, wing coverts are barred, primaries lean rufous, and secondaries use deep blue-black tones, all painted onto a high-resolution texture sheet to keep edges crisp across the different surface areas.

Working through texel density, I land around half a millimeter per texel, which is plenty sharp, and decide no ground or pedestal is needed since the brief doesn't call for one. For the fan feathers, I confirm the rachis spike sits centered through the card so it pokes through both faces, reading convincingly as leaded glass construction, and decide to skip adding extra lead-came arcs across layers.

I check whether a rose-window ornament at the fan's base would even be visible, but the body blocks it from the front so I leave it out. I'm tuning glow strength for the cards and jewel cabochons, and considering a crest/pompom glow too, while sketching out the lead-outline details around the eye decal and nostrils, and figuring the neck's lead collar line gets covered by paint anyway. Then I start tallying up the texture set needed: eye variants, crest tip, face eye, and a possible sword-feather fishtail treatment.

I settle on roughly five to six textures, skip the medallion idea, and note the double-sided cards work fine for stained glass since mirrored patterns look natural there. Writing feather barb SVG...

Still defining eye rings...

I'm also planning a sword/fishtail feather shape for the bottom-edge feathers, and working out how to batch card meshes by texture rather than generating one per feather call, since each texture should ideally produce a single combined mesh for efficiency.

I'm now estimating part counts: alternating textures by index parity gives natural overlap variation, eye jewels could stay as individual spheres per feather given the part budget is generous, and I'm tallying up body, neck, head, eyes, beak, nostril, and crest pieces toward a total part count.

Working through wings (sweep, membrane, primaries, secondaries), legs (trousers, toes, claws, spurs), and the fan (shafts, cards, jewels, rectrices) brings the estimate to roughly 225 parts, comfortably within the 180-340 target. I'm also checking triangle counts — reducing shaft sweep sides to keep the 82 shafts lightweight at around 8k triangles total — and considering adding leaded outline details on the wing panels.

I'm now planning to extrude lead-colored came edges along each feather blade's trailing edge for that classic stained-glass look, painting the extrusion walls dark while keeping the glass cells separate. Each blade gets its own paint capturing its thickness vector, and I'll add a thin lead stripe along the rachis centerline of each blade using the outline coordinates.

Similarly for membranes, I'm using along/across coordinates to paint the trailing rim as lead, keeping the body and other parts glass-only without extra 3D seams. I'm also verifying the lowest point of the model — toes sit near y=0 while the fan bottoms out around 0.46, so nothing should clip below the base.

Now I'm working through the builder API for the spine and hip joints, figuring out how to define the root hips joint and chain it into spine1 and chest tip positions with correct parenting and tangent-aligned orientation.

Next I'm setting up the neck chain with catmull-rom interpolation through four points, resampled into three joints (neck1-neck3), parented to chest, then placing the head joint at the end of the neck path with a forward-leaning direction vector.

Checking loft station format and bone list shape for the API, then sketching the skull as a scaled sphere attached to the head joint at HC. For facial decals, I'm planning to use the surface-around-and-at method on the skull to find hit points for placing symmetric features.

For mirroring, I need to work out which side faces the viewer — figuring out the normal direction at a given azimuth and cross-referencing it with the view direction and up vector to determine left/right orientation for decal placement.

Now I'm sketching the face SVG, placing the eye circle and drawing the white crescent stripes above and below it using curved paths to mimic the peacock's facial markings.

Positioning the beak cone relative to the head joint, working out the forward offset and aim direction so the base sits inside the skull and the tip projects out, then flattening it slightly with a local scale.

I'm checking that the upper and lower beak cones line up properly with the skull geometry so the mouth looks closed but not overlapping oddly. I'm adding small dark spheres for nostrils positioned on the upper beak sides, then moving on to the crest.

For the crest, I'm placing it near the top of the skull slightly forward, with a ring of radial directions spanning roughly -55 to 40 degrees so it fans forward and leans back a bit, each spike built as a thin four-sided shaft in a lead color.

Now I'm setting up tip cards sized small for each spike, finishing the wings, and moving on to legs. For the tail fan, I'm defining layered feather trains with varying counts, lengths, spread angles, and jeweled tips -- outer, middle, and inner layers, each progressively shorter and narrower.

I'm checking how the innermost layer's feathers emerge relative to the body's rump geometry, making sure feathers near the base don't clip through the body's half-width and instead poke out naturally from behind the rump.

Checking the lower feather angles confirms they stay within range, while layer A's spread extends well beyond the wingspan at those x-coordinates. I'm also working out the primary feather tip positions by extending from the wrist along their directional vectors.

Now I'm figuring out the tail feather ring: positioning it behind the body with a slight forward tilt to give a cupped look, using cone-shaped spikes for the rectrices even though they're mostly hidden from view anyway.

Explicitly binding each spike's bone to tailBase so it follows the main joint hierarchy correctly, then working out the fan axis direction and how card frames alternate texture and offset by parity for the feather layout.

For the shaft spike's taper, I'm reasoning about where the shaft should actually terminate relative to the card's eye -- since real feathers have the shaft running up into the eye, I'm shortening the shaft length to roughly L minus a third of the card length so it ends tucked within the eye rather than poking past it.

Now I'm placing a small sphere jewel at the eye center, computed as roughly 0.74 of the card length from the base, and flattening it along the world Z-axis with a non-uniform scale to mimic a cabochon shape since there's no local orientation to rely on -- then giving it a glowing blue tint to match the card's heart motif.

I realize `item.bone` could be null, so I should fall back to a default bone like `tailBase`, or better, use `item.moved(pt)` as a frame so the jewel inherits the item's orientation directly, letting me scale along local z to flatten it correctly relative to the card's forward direction. I wrap the part in a glow call with intensity 1.4, then move on to defining the card frames for the next feather layer.

Checking the width-to-length ratio for the cards against the drawing's aspect (60:200, so 0.3), I compute the outer layer width as 0.18 to stay undistorted, then work out the eye spacing at radius ~0.9 — 27 eyes across 196° gives roughly 7.25° or 0.114m apart, meaning the 0.18 width overlaps by about 0.066, which actually mimics how real fan feathers overlap. I'm now comparing how layer A and layer B's eye positions and card spans interact radially to make sure the barbs blend naturally between layers.

For the outer layer's first two and last two feather positions, I'm switching to a sword texture instead of the usual eye pattern, storing those into a separate frame list. Then I move on to sweeping the leg chain through the thigh and shin joints with tapering tube radii, applying the leg color, and shaping the trousers as a capsule between the hip and knee joints.

I'm now setting up the thigh capsule with a darker glass tint, confirming it inherits the hip joint's bone since the first endpoint determines bone attachment, and starting to compute the limb's root and target positions for the leg.

Working out the knee bending forward and the tibia angling back to the hock, keeping it tucked under the body's feathered trousers, then chaining the leg joints together with named parts for hip, knee, ankle, and foot and marking the foot as the ground contact point.

Now building the toes: spreading three forward-facing digits at slight angles plus a rear hallux, computing each tip position, creating joint and capsule bones for each toe, and adding small claw spikes at the tips.

Checking toe contact points against the ground plane, then moving to wing setup: positioning the chest and shoulder joints, sweeping arm radii for the wing taper, and attaching a membrane to the wing chain using the trailing edge points for the covert coloring.

Working out the primary feather outline shape with a tapered, sharp-tipped blade silhouette and confirming it has no self-intersections.

The thickness direction is computed by crossing the feather's forward axis with its orthogonal span axis, and the feather attaches at the wrist joint. I'm now setting up secondary feathers along the forearm between elbow and wrist, lerping base points and angling their direction downward and backward to match the membrane's trailing edge.

To avoid the overlap flicker, I'll shift the secondaries to start from the trailing edge points instead, offsetting slightly along the normal so they extend the wing cleanly rather than overlapping the membrane. I'm settling on having them originate directly from the trailing edge via a lerp, keyed to the elbow/wrist bone positions, while primaries continue to point outward-back from the wing-hand.

For the leading edge, I'll sweep a thin path along the trailing edge geometry skinned to the wing chain bone so it follows the joint motion naturally. For the covert feather bars, I'm computing a coloring pattern based on cell position (combining y and z coordinates into a periodic floor function) to alternate between cream and dark shading near the shoulder region.

Now I'm defining the body paint logic: a glass shader region that checks the cell's forward-facing position and vertical normal to decide whether a point should be colored blue (front/upper areas), belly tone (underside), or bronze (elsewhere), with the rump area trending greener. I'm also setting up a helper function to safely pick colors from a list by clamping the index.

I'm working out the lead line thickness—given the pane size and edge distance threshold, the lead border comes out to roughly 4mm wide, and I'm adjusting similar values for the neck region's smaller pane size.

For the crest tip, I'm designing a teardrop-shaped SVG icon with a short stalk at the bottom, using a turquoise outer fill with a dark lead-colored stroke, plus a smaller inner shape in deep blue to create a layered gem-like highlight effect.

Now I'm moving to the sword feather design -- envisioning long glass-shard barbs that widen into a fishtail "V" notch at the top, rendered in bronze-green tones. Writing feather SVG generator function...

I'm planning the eye's radial spokes clipped to the outer ellipse, shaping a kidney-like iris form, and laying out the draw order: barbs first, then the shaft line, then the outer fringe ellipse on top.

Continuing the layering—band, turquoise ring, spokes, inner ring, iris heart shape, then a small highlight and tiny white glint for sheen. I'm also planning to give the outer fringe ellipse a scalloped, jagged edge by generating a wavy polygon of alternating-radius points to mimic feather barbs.

I'll use a brown glass palette for the rectrix, keep the face untextured, and decide I only need around five or six distinct feather/texture variants total rather than adding unnecessary extras like a stained-glass emblem.

I consider adding lead came seams around the neck base where blue meets bronze, but that risks failing with the surface loop, so I'll skip it and stick with the lead lines already delineating wing covert edges. I'm importing the glow kit and double-checking the `cards` function's type signature to make sure frames and options line up correctly.

Working out type imports for Frame...

I'm setting up the leg sweep call with a tapering radius profile, then checking that the spine chain parents correctly to hips, adding a tailBase joint, and confirming the wing chain parents to chest off the spine tip.

For the neck and head, I'm parenting the neck chain to chest and sizing the head scale a bit larger than realistic proportions to keep the stylized bird look, making sure the neck sweep radius matches the skull width. Then I'm working on crest spikes radiating outward from the crown point with small shaft spikes and a tip card frame positioned via a local offset.

I'm figuring out the crest card orientation so the pompom fan reads correctly from a side view, choosing a flow direction along the x-axis with cross-facing enabled so the cards face sideways. I'm also bumping glow card strength to 1.2 and jotting down quick notes on leg paint and making the eye large enough to read clearly from the front.

Checking the eye position at a ±60 azimuth angle, I decide to narrow it to ±50 so it reads better from the front view. I'm also placing the rectrice spikes slightly behind layer A with brown glass paint, planning gaps in the fan cards so they peek through, and considering whether to add extra lead seam details or a web-like glass surface between the fan feathers.

Looking at coverage across the layered fan cards, I map out how layers A through D overlap at different radii so gaps near the shaft bases get filled in from the front, while the back view relies on the shafts alone since they're mostly hidden behind the body anyway.

Now I'm planning the actual implementation: importing only the needed helpers from the builder library, using rng to add slight random jitter to feather lengths and spin for a more natural look, and being careful to avoid unused imports or parameters since the typechecker flags those.

Writing glass material code...

Still verifying the type inference for the return array against the ColorInput tuple type...

For the blade glass paint, I'm writing a function that colors the lead border differently based on normal alignment with the thickness axis or proximity to the rachis centerline, falling back to the base paint elsewhere. For membrane, I'm defining edge detection near the border using the s coordinates to apply the lead color versus the covert pattern.

Now I'm setting up wing construction with mirrored left/right chains, defining a helper to flip x by sign, then building a catmull spline through points to shape each wing's primaries.

Still defining primary feather positions...

Now I'm placing secondary blades along the trailing edge at several points between t=0.15 and 0.85, with direction and orientation derived from the trail tangent so they extend outward from the membrane edge without overlapping it, binding each to the elbow or wrist bone depending on position.

I'm nudging the base slightly inward along the direction and thickness so there's a tiny coplanar overlap for a shimmer effect, then deciding to skip duplicating the lead rim paint along the secondaries and arm leading edge since the membrane sweep already handles it. I'm also noting that covert feathers need barred peacock-style patterning and confirming the rufous primary color matches real chestnut peacock primaries, then moving on to check the leg capsule geometry parameters.

Now I'm working out thigh capsules spanning from the hip joint down toward a point partway between knee and ankle for a plump trouser shape, rigged to the hip joint, colored in a dark bronze-grey glass tone, while body, neck, and head each get their own paint zones and toe/claw colors are being set.

For the rig, I'm assigning roles — legs as "leg", wings as "wing", toes as "digit", jaw as "jaw" — and deciding the train ring should use the "tail" role like the example rather than "fan". Then for the neck, I'm setting up a three-link chain starting inside the body, with tapering sweep radii and round caps so the base seats cleanly inside the body mesh.

Now I'm working through the head placement — defining a head center point just forward and up from where the neck ends, and realizing that "forward" and other directional words in this system refer to world-space directions tied to the model's orientation, not to the head's own local aim, so I need to use head.local with those fixed world directions regardless of how the head itself is angled.

Then I'm placing the beak: figuring the skull's front surface relative to the head center, positioning a cone for the beak so its base sits just inside the skull and its tip extends forward with a slight downward tilt, checking the numbers line up at roughly the skull's equator height. After that I start on the jaw joint position, offset slightly back and down from the beak base.

Working out the lower beak cone position relative to the jaw bone, checking its base and tip coordinates align with the upper beak tip, then setting both cones' radii and scaling so the upper and lower beak pieces overlap just enough at the jaw hinge. I'm planning nostril placement on the sides of the upper beak, eye decal angles, and about to start positioning the crest.

Now I'm figuring out the tail fan structure: setting up a ring of feather items parented to the tail base, with options for count, radius, angle range, and tilt, plus named joints for each item. I'm adding jittered shaft lengths using a seeded random function, and working through how each feather item's local position and orientation get computed within the ring callback.

For the jewel at the heart's center, I'm placing a flattened glowing sphere slightly offset forward in z so it sits in front of the card surface, matching the direction the item leans toward. The card itself faces forward along the flow direction, which keeps everything consistent.

Now I'm working out feather lengths for a natural fan shape—longer at the top center, shorter toward the sides, with some jitter for organic variation, and mapping each feather's angle across the fan range by its index. I'm also shrinking the card sizes proportionally with feather length, flagging the outermost feathers as "sword feathers" for a layer, and adding spike-shaped rectrices near the tail base.

I'm deciding against extra decorative touches like ankle cuffs, jewel studs, or neck beads, keeping focus on the eye ring decal and the white facial patch outline instead, and skipping the idea of decorative back struts on the fan. I'm also verifying that frame-based positioning handles orientation correctly and checking the card size parameters before continuing.

Now I'm verifying the import path and paint colors for the body and membrane, then working through the leg chain and IK structure to make sure the foot tip connects properly to the toe joints, checking that the toe positions don't overlap with other elements.

Confirming the inner toe spread leaves enough clearance from the foot center, then adding a small spur spike near the ankle and double-checking it doesn't collide with the wings. I'm setting up the crest ring frame and joint parented to the head, deciding to skip the collar detail, and verifying the body loft station positions.

Checking that the body's lower bound at the hip clears the leg attachment point, and confirming the wing shoulder placement sits within the body's width at that z-depth.

Feathers emerging at that body radius still fit fine, and the tail covert region keeps its bronze-green-with-gold paint. I'm adding a guard so the glow/cards call doesn't throw on empty frame arrays, then moving into writing the SVG template for feathers.

Writing feather SVG function...

Still writing fringe and spoke coordinates...

Still drawing the eye layers...
